extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, researchers and policymakers interested in comparative blasphemy laws and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative encyclopedic overview of how different jurisdictions define, criminalize, restrict, or repeal blasphemy-related conduct and the legal standards applied. Covers statutory elements, typical penalties, policy rationales, human-rights commentary, and notable case examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of blasphemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy is the act of insulting or showing contempt or lack of reverence to a deity, or sacred objects, or toward something considered sacred or inviolable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generic definition underpins many national laws but is implemented differently across jurisdictions (different thresholds for insult, contempt, reverence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection objective: protecting religious belief vs protecting individuals/public order
rubrics_metrics.description: Some states use blasphemy laws to protect the religious beliefs of a majority or to offer protection to minorities; others justify them as measures to maintain public order because such offenses 'have the tendency to lead to a breach of peace'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy justification affects scope and enforcement: laws framed to protect 'public order' may require a link to disturbance, whereas laws framed to protect beliefs may be broader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity / publication requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Many blasphemy or related offences require the act or statement to be public or to be disseminated (e.g., Germany §166 mentions 'publicly or by dissemination of writings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private expressions are often excluded; prosecution typically requires publication or public display/communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that act be 'suitable to disturb the public peace' or cause breach of public order
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes such as Germany's §166 criminalize defamation of religion 'in a manner suitable to disturb the public peace'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may assess likelihood of public disturbance; this narrows offences to speech/acts that risk unrest rather than mere offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent / purpose to offend
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws criminalize acts committed 'for the purpose of offending the religious feelings of believers' (e.g., Russian Article 148).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proving subjective intent can be required for conviction; in some regimes intent is an aggravating element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wounding or offending religious feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Several jurisdictions criminalize 'wounding religious feelings' or 'offending the religious feelings' of believers (phrases used in Seychelles, Poland, Philippines, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws framed this way focus on the emotional impact on adherents; courts may consider whether feelings were actually wounded and by how many adherents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location/time aggravation (places of worship / during religious ceremony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statutes (e.g., Philippines 'offending the religious feelings') specify that offences occur when acts are performed 'in a place devoted to religious worship or during the celebration of any religious ceremony'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offensive acts in sacred places or during ceremonies often carry harsher penalties or distinct offences because of heightened vulnerability of worship contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith / decency exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain laws contain explicit exemptions: e.g., Canada (former blasphemous libel provision) stated no conviction for 'expressing in good faith and in decent language, or attempting to establish by argument used in good faith and conveyed in decent language, an opinion on a religious subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-faith / decent-language provisions protect sincere criticism, academic debate, and reasoned argument; presence or absence of such exceptions greatly affects freedom-of-expression safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: protection of persons vs protection of divinities/doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some legal regimes protect people (adherents) rather than deities or doctrines; e.g., French law protects individuals/groups against defamation or insult but 'not the divinities'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether law aims at protecting believers or sacred objects influences constitutional compatibility and international human-rights assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold of offended adherents ('substantial number' requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain laws set or have been interpreted to require outrage among a 'substantial number of the adherents' for prosecution (Irish Defamation Act phrased the offence as 'grossly abusive or insulting ... thereby causing outrage among a substantial number of the adherents').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring a substantial-number threshold raises the bar for prosecution and guards against isolated complaints triggering criminal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factor: desecration of holy symbols or texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statutes impose stricter punishment where offending acts are coupled with desecration of holy symbols and/or religious texts (e.g., Russian law increases penalties when desecration is present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical desecration of objects or texts often elevates the culpability and penalties compared with verbal insult alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of penalties (fines, imprisonment, death sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Penalties across jurisdictions vary widely: fines, administrative penalties, imprisonment (months to years), and in some countries death sentences or capital penalties have been reported for blasphemy-related offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity of penalty correlates with law's scope and enforcement rigidity; international human-rights bodies criticize disproportionate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative vs criminal classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions treat blasphemy or public religious insult as an administrative offense punishable by fines (e.g., Italy's administrative fine framework), while others make it a criminal offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification affects procedural protections (criminal procedure, burden of proof, sentencing) and likelihood of prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vilification / religious insult vs hate-speech/incitement distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws may be framed as prohibiting 'vilification of religion', 'religious insult', 'defamation of religion', or as hate-speech prohibitions protecting individuals against incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence (ICCPR Art. 20).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International bodies generally recommend protecting individuals (from incitement) rather than religions/ideas per se; legal framing affects compatibility with free-expression norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of notoriety / 'notoriously offensive acts' wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Some statutes use language like 'performing acts notoriously offensive to the feelings of the faithful' (Philippines) which imports a notoriety or obvious offensiveness threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'notorious' qualifier can narrow offences to only clearly offensive acts; interpretation is context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial discretion / politically-mediated enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: In some states prosecution for blasphemy is discretionary or requires special initiation (e.g., New Zealand prosecutions historically were at Attorney-General discretion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion can act as a safeguard against frivolous cases but also introduce political variability and unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial / religion-specific limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some national laws historically protected only certain religions (e.g., Greek laws protecting Greek Orthodoxy), or were applied selectively in practice to majority faiths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religiously selective application raises constitutional equality concerns and may be vulnerable to challenge under nondiscrimination principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-criminal alternatives and civil penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: In jurisdictions where blasphemy prosecutions are rare or repealed, related protections may be enforced through civil law (defamation, discrimination, hate-speech civil remedies) or regulatory censorship rather than criminal sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifts from criminal to civil/regulatory mechanisms reflect attempts to balance expression and protection of persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical origin and doctrinal bases
rubrics_metrics.description: Many blasphemy laws derive from historic sources (e.g., English common law, Blasphemy Act 1697) and religiously-influenced moral codes (e.g., St. Thomas Aquinas' formulation in medieval French law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding historical origins helps explain present-day textual anomalies and regional exceptions (e.g., Alsace-Moselle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial interpretation and case examples as limiting principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Court decisions and high-profile prosecutions/acquittals (e.g., Gerard Reve, Monty Python's Life of Brian, Stephen Fry incident) shape how broadly statutes are read, often focusing on public order links, intent, or actual harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents may narrow enforcement in practice; examples in the article illustrate application nuances and defenses used.

rubrics_metrics.name: International human-rights guidance: restrict incitement, not criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 20 of the ICCPR requires states to adopt measures against 'any advocacy of national racial or religious hatred that constitutes incitement to discrimination, hostility or violence', while human-rights experts stress protections must be 'carefully circumscribed' and do not support a prohibition of blasphemy per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws compliant with international guidance typically target incitement to harm rather than mere criticism or insult of religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap and interaction with hate-speech and anti-discrimination laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries combine or coordinate blasphemy-type offences with hate-speech, anti-discrimination, or public-order statutes to address religiously motivated hostility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where overlap exists, enforcement may proceed under hate-speech frameworks that focus on protection of persons/groups rather than sacred ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness and abuse risk — 'vagueness' as a legal critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Several commentators and examples in the article note that vague phrasing (e.g., 'offends religious feelings') risks abuse and may unduly limit freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vagueness invites selective enforcement; legal reforms often aim to define elements (intent, publicity, consequence) to reduce misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform pathways: repeal, amendment, or symbolic repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The article documents different reform outcomes: full repeal (e.g., New Zealand, Norway), symbolic parliamentary acts (Alsace-Moselle repeal in France), or legislative weakening/exception insertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform options include removing criminal penalties, narrowing scope to incitement to violence, adding good-faith exceptions, or transferring matters to civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to art, satire and media
rubrics_metrics.description: National responses to artistic works (e.g., Life of Brian, satirical art, magazines) illustrate the test applied: whether a work is mere criticism/satire or crosses into unlawful provocation/disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and censors evaluate context, intent, public reaction, and connection to public order; artistic-value and satirical nature are common defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative procedures and local-level offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some localities impose municipal or local-bylaw penalties for public blasphemy (e.g., local ordinances in Italian towns), separate from national criminal codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local-level rules can persist even where national repeal has occurred; practitioners must check subnational law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special evidentiary and constitutional concerns (discrimination and equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Blasphemy offences that single out or disproportionately protect one religion may raise constitutional issues (discrimination on religious grounds) and conflict with bills of rights/free-expression provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may strike down discriminatory blasphemy provisions or require interpretive narrowing to comply with constitutional equality and free-speech guarantees.
